newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi ice-cream firm's dominance melting away.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi ice-cream firm's dominance melting away.

text.p: Thirty-six years after Four Seasons sold its first ice-cream on the edge of Hanoi's Hoan Kiem lake, the tiny state-owned company is seeing its market domination melting away.
"It's all ice and no cream these days," says a Hanoi resident and former patron. "It's OK, but people don't really go there now," says another.
Four Seasons is arguably the most famous ice-cream producer in northern Vietnam. In an impoverished country of only sparse luxuries it has managed to survive through decades of both war and neglect.
But 10 years after Vietnam launched its market-led reforms, the economic time-trap that once assured the unquestioned financial existence of such companies has gone.
"We are facing very tough competition these days," says Madame Le Minh Thuan, the firm's 41-year-old director.
"Foreign firms began to come in in the last three years, but we also have domestic competitors. They can re-equip and modernise. They have money."
Competition in the ice-cream business has indeed appeared in the Vietnamese capital in recent years, but among the newcomers, there are differing views of its intensity.
"It's very weather-sensitive here in Hanoi," says Nick Deans of U.S. firm Carvel, which recently set up a glitzy parlour just doors away.
"People are ice-cream crazy in the summer," he adds. "But, competitive? I'd say it's a market that's going to take time."

Carvel is just one of the new arrivals in Hanoi. Allied Domecq's Baskin-Robbins ice-cream company, complete with a home-delivery service, sundaes and cakes has also opened a store just around the corner.

Like many executives in Vietnam, Thuan shies away from talking detail about her business. The firm has around 400 customers a day, which at roughly $1.50 an ice-cream, would ring up sales of around $3,600 per week.
"It's not very profitable, but we do make some money," she says.
But viewed in conventional terms, Four Seasons ought to be doing better.
Its recently refurbished restaurant, in a French-style building, enjoys a prime location in the heart of the capital.
Many of its products, jackfruit or green-rice ice cream for example, are distinctly Vietnamese. Added to that it's cheap.
Despite its strengths, however, the tiny Hanoi firm is feeling the pressure of new market forces, along with thousands of other enterprises in Vietnam like it.

"At the moment small companies like this are growing fast and account for about 60 percent of GDP (gross domestic product) and 70 percent of employment," says Hoang Van Dung of Vietnam's Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI).
"But in reality both state and private enterprises have problems. Problems with capital, problems with technology and problems with marketing know-how."
Four Seasons runs the entire gamut of the difficulties Dung describes, with a few more thrown in.
In order to stay in business the company is diversifying into areas which risk diluting its 36 years of expertise.
Thuan says the company hopes to expand its ground-floor premises and start selling Western-style fast foods such as hamburgers and soft drinks.

In addition Four Seasons is getting into the property business. In a backyard immediately behind the street-facade restaurant, workmen are hammering together a building which will eventually be rented out as office space.

"This is typical," says VCCI's Dung. "The competition is exposing them to Western or Asian business practices they've not seen before. The local people see this... but still they just do what they want."
